Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN) -- For a world-class shopping experience you should head to glitzy Ginza. As well as flagship fashion outlets, the area boasts one of the city's best department stores, Mitsukoshi (4-6-16 Chuo Dori). The real treat here, as at many Tokyo department stores, is the fantastic basement-level food hall ("depachika"). For the complete Mitsukoshi experience, there's an ever bigger store in Nihombashi. The "Electric Town" of Akihabara is tech-head's heaven. Next door is Matsuya, another big department store, and while you're in the area don't miss the Sony Building (5-3-1 Ginza, Chuo-ku). Your inner games geek won't be able to resist the entire floor devoted to the PlayStation. If you've ever wondered where Tokyo teenagers buy their wacky cyber-goth manga-inspired attire, the answer is Takeshita-Dori, a narrow street in Harajuku. On Sundays the street fills with fashion-conscious teens, dressed to impress. For the less adventurous, but more discerning shopper, Harajuku's main thoroughfare, Omotesando is lined with elegant boutiques, including Louis Vuitton, Prada and Loveless (3-17-11 Minami-Aoyama). Looking unlike any shop you've seen before, Loveless has three floors of hip Japanese clothing and a basement decked out like the dungeon of some deranged medieval aristocrat. Harajuku is also home to six-floor Kiddy Land (6-1-9 Jingu-mae), one of the city's best toy stores, with a huge selection of Hello Kitty products. The area around Shibuya Station is a buzzing epicenter of shopping activity. Among its highlights are Tokyu Hands (Takashimaya Times Square, 5-24-2 Sendagaya), a department store that sells everything you could ever need, and plenty of stuff you had no idea even existed (electrically heated pilllows anyone?). A Bathing Ape (1 - Rise Bld. 13-17 Udagawa-Cho) offers funky T-shirts and trainers in an art gallery-style space, and Mandarake (Shibuya Beam B2 31-2 Udagawacho) is the place to satisfy your manga cravings, should you have any. For more manga, and a glimpse into the future, you'll want to go to Akihabara. Also known as Electric Town, Akihabara is a district of electronics stores clad in illuminated signs. Visit after dark for the full "Blade Runner" experience. Yodobashi Camera sells everything from next generation cell phones to cameras that aren't yet available outside Japan. For something more sedate, Daikanyama is a refined area popular with in-the-know fashionistas, while Jimbocho is the city's used-book quarter. Marunouchi was once a drab business district but is fast becoming the city's hottest shopping area. Shin-Marunouchi (just opposite the Marunouchi exit of Tokyo Stations) is a huge building, with the lowest seven floors devoted to chic shopping. The basement "depachika" is a feast for foodies. Tokyo International Forum (5-1 Marunouchi 3-chome, Chiyoda-ku) is a vast space used for art exhibitions and as a concert hall. It also boasts excellent shopping and hosts a flea market every other Sunday. Where to stay | What to see | Where to be seen | Where to eat | Where to shop . ...................... Do you agree with our Tokyo picks? Send us your comments and suggestions in the "Sound Off" box below and we'll print the best.

Alongside major designer flagship stores, the district is home to Mitsukoshi, one of Tokyo’s finest department stores, at 4-6-16 Chuo Dori. As with many department stores in the city, the highlight is its superb basement food floor, known as a “depachika.” For an even fuller Mitsukoshi outing, visit the larger branch in Nihombashi.

Akihabara, often called “Electric Town,” is paradise for technology lovers. Nearby you’ll find Matsuya, another large department store, and while visiting Ginza, be sure to stop by the Sony Building at 5-3-1 Ginza, Chuo-ku. Anyone with a soft spot for gaming will find it hard to pass up the floor entirely dedicated to PlayStation.

If you’ve ever asked yourself where Tokyo’s teenagers pick up their eccentric cyber-goth, manga-influenced clothes, the answer is Takeshita-Dori, a slim street in Harajuku. On Sundays, it becomes packed with style-minded young people dressed to stand out.

Shoppers with more restrained but sophisticated tastes should head to Omotesando, Harajuku’s main avenue, where refined boutiques line the street. These include Louis Vuitton, Prada and Loveless at 3-17-11 Minami-Aoyama. Loveless looks unlike almost any store you’re likely to have visited, offering three levels of fashionable Japanese clothing plus a basement designed like the dungeon of a deranged medieval noble.

Harajuku is also where you’ll find the six-story Kiddy Land at 6-1-9 Jingu-mae, one of Tokyo’s best toy shops, with an enormous range of Hello Kitty merchandise.

The streets surrounding Shibuya Station form a lively center of retail energy. Notable stops include Tokyu Hands at Takashimaya Times Square, 5-24-2 Sendagaya, a department store selling practically everything you might need, along with many items you never knew existed — electrically warmed pillows, for example. A Bathing Ape, located at 1 - Rise Bld. 13-17 Udagawa-Cho, sells bold T-shirts and sneakers in a space arranged like an art gallery. Mandarake, at Shibuya Beam B2 31-2 Udagawacho, is the place to go if you want to indulge a taste for manga.

For still more manga, as well as a sense of what the future might look like, head to Akihabara. Also known as Electric Town, the district is packed with electronics shops covered in glowing signs. Visit at night for the full “Blade Runner” atmosphere. Yodobashi Camera carries everything from next-generation mobile phones to cameras not yet sold outside Japan.

For a calmer shopping experience, Daikanyama offers an elegant atmosphere favored by well-informed fashion devotees, while Jimbocho is Tokyo’s district for secondhand books.

Marunouchi, formerly a dull business area, is rapidly turning into one of the city’s most exciting shopping districts. Shin-Marunouchi, directly across from the Marunouchi exit of Tokyo Station, is a massive complex whose bottom seven floors are devoted to stylish retail. Its basement “depachika” is a delight for food lovers.

Tokyo International Forum, at 5-1 Marunouchi 3-chome, Chiyoda-ku, is an enormous venue used for art exhibitions and concerts. It also features strong shopping options and holds a flea market every other Sunday.

outputs.L3:
Tokyo is one of the world’s great shopping cities, with each neighborhood offering a distinct atmosphere and specialty. From luxury fashion and refined department stores to electronics, youth culture, toys, and manga, the city provides an extraordinary range of retail experiences.

Ginza is the place to go for a polished, world-class shopping experience. This elegant district is home to flagship fashion stores, luxury brands, and some of Tokyo’s most prestigious retail spaces. A highlight is Mitsukoshi, one of Japan’s most famous department stores, where visitors can browse high-quality fashion, cosmetics, gifts, and household goods. Ginza’s department stores are also known for their impressive basement food halls, where beautifully presented sweets, bento boxes, delicacies, and gourmet ingredients make shopping as much about food as fashion.

For those interested in technology, electronics, gaming, and pop culture, Akihabara is a must-visit. Known as Tokyo’s “Electric Town,” the area is packed with electronics shops selling everything from cameras and computer parts to the latest gadgets. It is also a major destination for gaming enthusiasts, anime fans, and collectors, with stores dedicated to video games, figurines, manga, and character merchandise. Akihabara’s bright signs, multi-floor specialty shops, and energetic atmosphere make it one of Tokyo’s most distinctive districts.

Harajuku offers a very different kind of shopping experience, especially around Takeshita-Dori. This famous pedestrian street is closely associated with teenage fashion, including cyber-goth, kawaii, cosplay, and manga-inspired styles. It is colorful, crowded, and full of small shops selling inexpensive clothing, accessories, and novelty items. Nearby Omotesando provides a more refined contrast, with tree-lined avenues, elegant boutiques, designer stores, and stylish cafés. Together, Harajuku and Omotesando show both the playful and sophisticated sides of Tokyo fashion.

Harajuku is also home to several unique stores that make the area especially memorable. Loveless is known for stylish, hip Japanese clothing and carefully selected contemporary fashion, attracting shoppers looking for something more distinctive than mainstream brands. Kiddy Land is another essential stop, especially for visitors interested in toys, character goods, and Japanese pop culture. Its floors are filled with playful merchandise, including Hello Kitty products and other beloved characters, making it popular with both children and adults.

Around Shibuya Station, shoppers will find one of Tokyo’s busiest and most diverse retail hubs. The area is filled with department stores, fashion outlets, record shops, bookstores, and specialty retailers. Tokyu Hands is a favorite for practical and creative goods, offering everything from stationery and craft supplies to homeware and travel accessories. A Bathing Ape appeals to fans of Japanese streetwear, while Mandarake is a treasure trove for manga, anime, collectibles, and pop-culture items. With its constant energy and wide variety of shops, Shibuya is an ideal place to explore Tokyo’s eclectic retail scene.

Together, Ginza, Akihabara, Harajuku, Omotesando, and Shibuya reveal the remarkable diversity of shopping in Tokyo. Whether you are searching for luxury brands, cutting-edge electronics, youth fashion, designer boutiques, character goods, or rare manga, each district offers its own unique version of the city’s shopping culture.
outputs.L4:
Tokyo is one of the world’s great shopping cities, offering everything from elegant department stores and luxury fashion houses to tiny specialty boutiques, electronics megastores, toy shops, streetwear outlets, and manga stores. Each district has its own atmosphere and focus, making shopping in Tokyo feel less like a single activity and more like a journey through different sides of the city’s culture. Whether you are looking for designer clothes, gourmet food, anime goods, the latest gadgets, or trend-setting youth fashion, Tokyo has a neighborhood that feels made for you.

Ginza is one of Tokyo’s most famous shopping districts and is best known for luxury, refinement, and long-established department stores. Its wide boulevards are lined with flagship boutiques from international fashion houses, as well as sophisticated Japanese brands. Department stores such as Mitsukoshi and Matsuya Ginza offer high-end clothing, cosmetics, accessories, and home goods, while their basement food halls are destinations in their own right. These gourmet floors are filled with beautifully packaged sweets, seasonal delicacies, prepared meals, tea, sake, and premium ingredients. Ginza is also a good area for shoppers interested in stationery, art supplies, jewelry, and carefully crafted gifts. The overall experience is polished and elegant, making it ideal for those who enjoy classic department-store shopping and luxury browsing.

Akihabara, by contrast, is Tokyo’s center for electronics, gaming, anime, and manga culture. Once known mainly for its electronics shops, the district is still a major destination for computers, cameras, audio equipment, parts, and gadgets. Large electronics retailers offer several floors of products, from household appliances to gaming consoles and mobile accessories. At the same time, Akihabara has become one of the best-known places in Japan for fans of anime, manga, and video games. Visitors can find stores packed with figures, model kits, trading cards, character goods, retro games, and comics. Some shops specialize in new merchandise, while others sell secondhand collectibles that are difficult to find elsewhere. For anyone interested in Japanese pop culture, Akihabara is one of the most exciting places to explore.

Harajuku offers a completely different kind of shopping experience. Famous for youth fashion and colorful street style, the area is closely associated with creativity, self-expression, and subcultures. Takeshita Street is one of the district’s busiest shopping streets, filled with small fashion shops, accessory stores, crepe stands, and novelty boutiques. It is especially popular with teenagers and visitors looking for playful, affordable fashion. Beyond Takeshita Street, Harajuku also has more refined and independent shops, including vintage stores, sneaker boutiques, and brands that mix streetwear with Japanese design. The neighborhood is a good place to see how Tokyo’s younger generations experiment with fashion, from cute and colorful styles to edgy, alternative looks.

Nearby Omotesando is more polished and architectural, often compared to a luxury shopping avenue. The broad, tree-lined street is home to designer boutiques, stylish shopping complexes, and carefully designed flagship stores. Omotesando Hills is one of the area’s major retail landmarks, offering fashion, beauty, lifestyle goods, and restaurants in a sleek modern setting. Many international luxury brands have stores in Omotesando, but the district also features Japanese designers, concept shops, and select stores with a strong sense of taste and curation. Compared with the energy of Harajuku, Omotesando feels calmer and more sophisticated, making it a good destination for shoppers interested in fashion, design, and lifestyle products.

Shibuya is one of Tokyo’s busiest and most energetic shopping areas. Centered around Shibuya Station and the famous scramble crossing, the district is packed with department stores, fashion buildings, record shops, cosmetics stores, and entertainment complexes. Shibuya is especially popular with young adults and trend-conscious shoppers. Large retail centers offer floors of casual fashion, shoes, accessories, beauty products, and lifestyle goods. The area is also a strong destination for music, streetwear, and youth culture. Shibuya’s shopping scene changes quickly, reflecting current trends in fashion, entertainment, and social media. Its lively streets, bright signs, and constant crowds make it one of the most recognizable images of modern Tokyo.

What makes shopping in Tokyo so distinctive is the variety between districts. A visitor can spend the morning exploring luxury stores and elegant food halls in Ginza, then travel to Akihabara for electronics and manga, continue to Harajuku for youth fashion and accessories, browse sophisticated boutiques in Omotesando, and finish the day in Shibuya among crowds, music, and trend-driven shops. Each neighborhood has a clear identity, yet together they show the range of Tokyo’s consumer culture.

Tokyo’s shops also stand out for their attention to detail. Department stores are known for excellent service, careful presentation, and beautifully wrapped purchases. Specialty shops often focus deeply on a single category, whether that is fountain pens, cameras, sneakers, toys, tea, or character merchandise. Even casual shopping can feel memorable because products are displayed thoughtfully and staff often take pride in helping customers find exactly what they need.

For travelers, Tokyo is not only a place to buy things but also a place to observe culture through shopping. Luxury fashion, traditional craftsmanship, pop culture, street style, electronics, and gourmet food all exist side by side. This diversity makes the city appealing to many kinds of shoppers: fashion lovers, collectors, technology enthusiasts, families, anime fans, food lovers, and anyone who enjoys discovering unusual or beautifully made products.

In the end, Tokyo’s shopping scene is one of the city’s greatest attractions. Its major districts each offer a different experience, from Ginza’s elegance to Akihabara’s gadget-filled energy, Harajuku’s playful youth culture, Omotesando’s stylish sophistication, and Shibuya’s fast-moving trends. Together, they make Tokyo a distinctive and exciting destination where shopping becomes a way to explore the character of the city itself.

## Where to shop in Tokyo: Seven neighborhoods worth packing an extra suitcase for

Tokyo doesn’t do “shopping district” in a casual way. Each neighborhood has its own retail identity — polished luxury, teenage streetwear, electronics overload, indie bookshops, or design-forward boutiques tucked into quiet lanes. Here are seven of the city’s best areas to browse, buy and linger.

---

### Ginza: Luxury flagships and immaculate department stores

Tokyo’s most glamorous shopping district is Ginza, where global fashion houses, historic department stores and high-concept retail spaces line broad, polished avenues. Even if you’re only window-shopping, the architecture and presentation are part of the experience.

**Where to go**

- **Ginza Six**  
  A major luxury complex with fashion, beauty, art installations and a rooftop garden.  
  **Address:** 6-10-1 Ginza, Chuo-ku, Tokyo

- **Mitsukoshi Ginza**  
  A classic Japanese department store with cosmetics, fashion, gifts and an excellent basement food hall.  
  **Address:** 4-6-16 Ginza, Chuo-ku, Tokyo

- **Itoya Ginza**  
  A must-visit for stationery lovers, with elegant notebooks, pens, paper goods and design items.  
  **Address:** 2-7-15 Ginza, Chuo-ku, Tokyo

- **UNIQLO Ginza**  
  One of the brand’s major Tokyo flagships, spread over multiple floors.  
  **Address:** 6-9-5 Ginza, Chuo-ku, Tokyo

**Best for:** Luxury fashion, cosmetics, stationery, refined gifts.

---

### Harajuku: Streetwear, youth culture and kawaii chaos

Harajuku is Tokyo’s playground for fashion experimentation. Takeshita Street delivers the famous crush of crepe stands, character goods and trend-driven boutiques, while nearby Cat Street offers a calmer, cooler mix of streetwear and vintage.

**Where to go**

- **Laforet Harajuku**  
  A long-running fashion complex packed with Japanese youth labels, accessories and edgy boutiques.  
  **Address:** 1-11-6 Jingumae, Shibuya-ku, Tokyo

- **WEGO Harajuku Takeshita-dori Store**  
  Affordable streetwear, accessories and trend pieces popular with younger shoppers.  
  **Address:** 1-19-19 Jingumae, Shibuya-ku, Tokyo

- **Kiddy Land Harajuku**  
  A multi-floor character-goods paradise with Sanrio, Studio Ghibli, Snoopy and more.  
  **Address:** 6-1-9 Jingumae, Shibuya-ku, Tokyo

- **Ragtag Harajuku**  
  A strong stop for secondhand designer fashion and Japanese labels.  
  **Address:** 6-14-2 Jingumae, Shibuya-ku, Tokyo

**Best for:** Street fashion, character goods, accessories, vintage finds.

---

### Shibuya: Big brands, sneakers and youth retail at full volume

Shibuya is Tokyo shopping with the volume turned up: giant screens, packed crossings, multi-level malls and a steady stream of trend-conscious locals. It’s ideal for one-stop shopping, especially if you want fashion, records, cosmetics or sneakers.

**Where to go**

- **Shibuya Parco**  
  A fashion and culture complex with designer boutiques, Japanese labels, pop-culture shops and restaurants.  
  **Address:** 15-1 Udagawacho, Shibuya-ku, Tokyo

- **Shibuya 109**  
  A landmark of Japanese youth fashion, especially women’s trendwear and accessories.  
  **Address:** 2-29-1 Dogenzaka, Shibuya-ku, Tokyo

- **Tower Records Shibuya**  
  One of Tokyo’s essential music stores, with CDs, vinyl, books, merch and events.  
  **Address:** 1-22-14 Jinnan, Shibuya-ku, Tokyo

- **Nintendo Tokyo**  
  Official Nintendo merchandise inside Shibuya Parco.  
  **Address:** Shibuya Parco 6F, 15-1 Udagawacho, Shibuya-ku, Tokyo

- **ABC-MART Grand Stage Shibuya**  
  A good stop for sneakers and casual footwear.  
  **Address:** 31-1 Udagawacho, Shibuya-ku, Tokyo

**Best for:** Youth fashion, sneakers, music, pop culture, cosmetics.

---

### Akihabara: Electronics, anime and collectibles

Akihabara is Tokyo’s electric town, a dense grid of gadget shops, gaming stores, anime retailers and collectible treasure troves. It can feel overwhelming, but that’s part of the appeal: rare figures, retro games and obscure cables may all be within the same block.

**Where to go**

- **Yodobashi Camera Multimedia Akiba**  
  A huge electronics store selling cameras, appliances, games, watches, toys and more.  
  **Address:** 1-1 Kanda Hanaokacho, Chiyoda-ku, Tokyo

- **Mandarake Complex**  
  Multi-floor secondhand manga, anime goods, toys, figures and collectibles.  
  **Address:** 3-11-12 Sotokanda, Chiyoda-ku, Tokyo

- **Super Potato Akihabara**  
  A beloved retro game shop with vintage consoles, cartridges and arcade nostalgia.  
  **Address:** 1-11-2 Sotokanda, Chiyoda-ku, Tokyo

- **Animate Akihabara**  
  Anime, manga, character goods and limited-edition merchandise.  
  **Address:** 4-3-2 Sotokanda, Chiyoda-ku, Tokyo

- **Akihabara Radio Kaikan**  
  A landmark building filled with hobby shops, figures, cards, models and collectibles.  
  **Address:** 1-15-16 Sotokanda, Chiyoda-ku, Tokyo

**Best for:** Electronics, anime, manga, retro games, figurines, hobby goods.

---

### Daikanyama: Design boutiques, lifestyle shops and slow browsing

Daikanyama is quieter and more polished than nearby Shibuya, with leafy lanes, independent boutiques and cafes built for lingering. It’s the neighborhood for tasteful homewares, books, ceramics, fashion and design objects.

**Where to go**

- **Daikanyama T-Site / Tsutaya Books**  
  One of Tokyo’s most beautiful bookstore complexes, with art, design, travel, magazines, music and cafes.  
  **Address:** 17-5 Sarugakucho, Shibuya-ku, Tokyo

- **Okura**  
  Japanese indigo-dyed clothing, workwear-inspired pieces and traditional textiles.  
  **Address:** 20-11 Sarugakucho, Shibuya-ku, Tokyo

- **Hollywood Ranch Market**  
  Casual fashion with a Japanese-Americana feel, denim and lifestyle goods.  
  **Address:** 28-17 Sarugakucho, Shibuya-ku, Tokyo

- **Hender Scheme Sukima Daikanyama**  
  Leather goods and footwear from the cult Japanese brand.  
  **Address:** 2-17 Sarugakucho, Shibuya-ku, Tokyo

**Best for:** Books, design, Japanese fashion, lifestyle goods, refined souvenirs.

---

### Jimbocho: Bookstores, vintage prints and literary wandering

Jimbocho is Tokyo’s book town, where narrow streets are lined with shops selling new, used, rare and specialist titles. Even if you don’t read Japanese, it’s a rewarding neighborhood for photography books, art catalogues, maps, ukiyo-e prints and vintage magazines.

**Where to go**

- **Kitazawa Bookstore**  
  Known for English-language books, humanities titles and a beautifully old-world atmosphere.  
  **Address:** 2-5 Kanda Jimbocho, Chiyoda-ku, Tokyo

- **Isseido Booksellers**  
  A historic shop specializing in rare books, academic works, prints and antiquarian volumes.  
  **Address:** 1-7 Kanda Jimbocho, Chiyoda-ku, Tokyo

- **Sanseido Bookstore Jimbocho Main Store**  
  A major Japanese bookstore and neighborhood landmark.  
  **Address:** 1-1 Kanda Jimbocho, Chiyoda-ku, Tokyo

- **Bohemian’s Guild**  
  Art books, photography, design titles and vintage magazines.  
  **Address:** 1-1 Kanda Jimbocho, Chiyoda-ku, Tokyo

**Best for:** Rare books, art books, photography, maps, vintage magazines.

---

### Marunouchi: Elegant malls and polished urban shopping

Between Tokyo Station and the Imperial Palace, Marunouchi is sleek, convenient and quietly luxurious. The area is perfect for shopping before a train departure, browsing Japanese lifestyle brands or finding a well-designed gift without plunging into a crowded youth district.

**Where to go**

- **Marunouchi Building / Maru Biru**  
  Fashion, lifestyle shops, restaurants and city views near Tokyo Station.  
  **Address:** 2-4-1 Marunouchi, Chiyoda-ku, Tokyo

- **Shin-Marunouchi Building / Shin-Marubiru**  
  A stylish retail and dining complex with boutiques, accessories and home goods.  
  **Address:** 1-5-1 Marunouchi, Chiyoda-ku, Tokyo

- **KITTE Marunouchi**  
  A beautifully renovated former post office building with Japanese craft, design, fashion and food.  
  **Address:** 2-7-2 Marunouchi, Chiyoda-ku, Tokyo

- **Tokyo Station Ichibangai**  
  Underground shopping packed with character stores, sweets and souvenir shops.  
  **Address:** 1-9-1 Marunouchi, Chiyoda-ku, Tokyo

- **Daimaru Tokyo**  
  A major department store directly connected to Tokyo Station, especially useful for gifts and food halls.  
  **Address:** 1-9-1 Marunouchi, Chiyoda-ku, Tokyo

**Best for:** Elegant gifts, department-store shopping, Japanese design, station souvenirs.

---

### Quick shopping tips for Tokyo

- **Bring your passport** for tax-free shopping at participating stores.  
- **Check floor guides** in department stores; the best food and gift sections are often in the basement.  
- **Carry cash**, especially for smaller vintage, book and hobby shops.  
- **Go early on weekends** in Harajuku, Shibuya and Akihabara to avoid peak crowds.  
- **Confirm opening hours** before visiting, as stores and specialty shops may change schedules.

# Where to shop in Tokyo

Tokyo doesn’t simply sell things — it stages entire worlds around them. A shopping day here can begin beneath the chandeliers of a century-old department store, detour through a multi-story manga labyrinth, and end with a jewel-box dessert from a basement food hall wrapped so beautifully it feels almost rude to open.

For classic retail theater, start in **Ginza**, where flagship department stores such as **Mitsukoshi**, **Matsuya** and **GINZA SIX** mix luxury labels with Japanese craftsmanship, design goods and immaculate service. Even if you’re not splurging on fashion, the depachika — basement food halls — are essential: rows of lacquered bento, seasonal wagashi sweets, fruit arranged like fine jewelry and takeaway sushi that puts many restaurants elsewhere to shame.

Pop culture pilgrims should head for **Akihabara** and **Ikebukuro**. Akihabara remains Tokyo’s best-known electronics district, with camera gear, gaming hardware, retro consoles, computer parts and gadget-stuffed shops stacked along neon-lit streets. Nearby manga and anime stores offer everything from new releases and character goods to rare collectibles. In Ikebukuro, **Otome Road** caters especially to fans of anime, manga and cosplay, with specialty shops that reward slow browsing.

For fashion, Tokyo’s personality shifts neighborhood by neighborhood. **Harajuku** still champions youth culture, vintage finds and experimental streetwear, while **Omotesando** offers architectural flagships and polished boutiques. **Daikanyama** and **Nakameguro** are quieter, with independent labels, lifestyle stores and cafes that make shopping feel like a leisurely urban wander.

Toy lovers — and nostalgic adults — should carve out time for **Kiddy Land** in Harajuku, a multi-floor celebration of Japanese and international characters, from Sanrio and Studio Ghibli favorites to limited-edition collectibles. For a more grown-up treasure hunt, Tokyo’s specialty stores and secondhand shops can turn up everything from designer vinyl figures to meticulously preserved model trains.

The secret to shopping in Tokyo is not to rush. The city rewards curiosity: step into the basement, take the elevator to the top floor, follow the tiny sign down a side street. In Tokyo, the best souvenir may be the thing you didn’t know existed until five minutes before you bought it.

# Tokyo Shopping Guide for Tourists

Tokyo is one of the world’s best shopping cities, with everything from luxury department stores and cutting-edge electronics to anime collectibles, street fashion, stationery, toys, and design goods. The city is best explored by neighborhood, since each area has its own style and specialty.

---

## 1. Ginza: Luxury, Department Stores & Design

### Mitsukoshi Ginza
**Best for:** Luxury shopping, cosmetics, food gifts, traditional Japanese goods  
**Area:** Ginza

Mitsukoshi is one of Japan’s most famous and historic department store chains, and the Ginza branch is a classic stop for tourists. It offers high-end fashion, beauty products, jewelry, homeware, and beautifully packaged Japanese gifts.

Do not miss the **depachika**, the basement food hall. It is ideal for browsing premium sweets, bento boxes, fruit, tea, wagashi Japanese confectionery, and elegant souvenirs. Many items are beautifully boxed, making them excellent gifts to bring home.

**Tourist tip:** Bring your passport. Many department stores offer tax-free shopping for foreign visitors, usually above a minimum purchase amount.

---

### Sony Building / Ginza Sony Park
**Best for:** Technology, design, Sony brand experiences  
**Area:** Ginza

The original Sony Building in Ginza was a longtime landmark for tech lovers. It was replaced by the **Ginza Sony Park** project, which continues Sony’s presence in the area through exhibitions, events, product showcases, and cultural experiences.

Rather than a traditional electronics shop, this is more of a brand and design destination. Check ahead for current exhibits, pop-ups, or limited-time events. It is especially worthwhile if you enjoy modern Japanese design, music, gaming, cameras, or Sony’s entertainment culture.

**Nearby:** Ginza’s luxury boutiques, Mitsukoshi, UNIQLO Ginza, and department stores are all within walking distance.

---

## 2. Harajuku: Youth Fashion, Cute Culture & Character Goods

### Takeshita-Dori
**Best for:** Youth fashion, accessories, crepes, cute souvenirs  
**Area:** Harajuku

Takeshita-Dori is Harajuku’s most famous shopping street. It is colorful, crowded, energetic, and especially popular with teenagers and young tourists. You will find small fashion boutiques, accessory shops, idol goods, character items, cosmetics, and snack stands.

This is also a great place to try Harajuku-style sweets, especially colorful crepes, rainbow cotton candy, and trendy drinks.

**What to expect:**  
- Very busy on weekends and holidays  
- Affordable fashion and accessories  
- Lots of photo-friendly shops and snacks  
- A fun but crowded atmosphere

**Best time to visit:** Weekday mornings or early afternoons if you want fewer crowds.

---

### Omotesando
**Best for:** Designer fashion, architecture, cafes, lifestyle shops  
**Area:** Harajuku/Aoyama

A short walk from Takeshita-Dori, Omotesando offers a completely different shopping experience. Often compared to a Japanese version of the Champs-Élysées, Omotesando is lined with trees, luxury boutiques, stylish malls, and modern architecture.

You will find international designer brands, Japanese fashion labels, upscale cosmetics, interior design shops, and elegant cafes. It is ideal for travelers who want a more refined shopping atmosphere after exploring Harajuku’s playful side.

**Good stops in the area:**  
- Omotesando Hills for fashion and design  
- Cat Street, between Harajuku and Shibuya, for streetwear and independent boutiques  
- Stylish coffee shops and dessert cafes

---

### Kiddy Land
**Best for:** Toys, character goods, Sanrio, Studio Ghibli, Pokémon-style gifts  
**Area:** Harajuku/Omotesando

Kiddy Land is one of Tokyo’s most beloved toy and character goods stores. The Harajuku branch is especially popular with tourists. It has multiple floors filled with plush toys, stationery, collectibles, anime and manga characters, kawaii items, and limited-edition goods.

You can find merchandise from popular Japanese and international characters, often including Sanrio, Rilakkuma, Sumikko Gurashi, Snoopy, Disney, Studio Ghibli, and more.

**Why visit:** Even if you are not shopping for children, Kiddy Land is a fun cultural experience and a great place to buy light, easy-to-pack souvenirs.

---

## 3. Shibuya & Shinjuku: Variety Shopping and Lifestyle Goods

### Tokyu Hands / Hands
**Best for:** Stationery, travel goods, DIY, kitchenware, beauty, lifestyle products  
**Areas:** Shibuya, Shinjuku, Ikebukuro, and other locations

Formerly known as Tokyu Hands and now often branded simply as **Hands**, this is one of Japan’s best shops for practical and creative goods. Tourists love it because the product range is huge and very Japanese in style.

You can shop for high-quality stationery, pens, notebooks, craft supplies, travel accessories, luggage organizers, cosmetics, kitchen tools, bento goods, home items, umbrellas, and quirky inventions.

**Recommended buys:**  
- Japanese pens and notebooks  
- Compact travel accessories  
- Bento boxes and kitchen gadgets  
- Nail care and beauty tools  
- Unique gifts and souvenirs

**Tip:** Set aside enough time. Hands stores are multi-floor and easy to get lost in.

---

## 4. Akihabara: Electronics, Anime, Games & Collectibles

### Yodobashi Camera
**Best for:** Electronics, cameras, appliances, games, watches, toys  
**Area:** Akihabara, Shinjuku, Ueno, and more

Yodobashi Camera is a major electronics retailer, and the **Yodobashi Akiba** store near Akihabara Station is one of the best and biggest. It offers cameras, lenses, computers, headphones, smartphones, gaming consoles, beauty appliances, rice cookers, watches, toys, and household electronics.

Many products are tourist-friendly, and some cameras or electronics may have international models. Staff may speak some English, especially in major branches, though this varies.

**Important tips:**  
- Check voltage compatibility before buying appliances. Japan uses 100V.  
- Ask whether the product has English menus or international warranty.  
- Bring your passport for tax-free purchases.  
- Compare prices if buying expensive electronics.

Yodobashi is also useful for non-electronics shopping, including capsule toys, model kits, stationery, and travel gadgets.

---

### Mandarake
**Best for:** Manga, anime goods, figures, doujinshi, retro toys, collectibles  
**Areas:** Akihabara, Nakano Broadway, Shibuya, Ikebukuro

Mandarake is a legendary secondhand and collectible chain specializing in manga, anime, figures, games, idol goods, cosplay items, art books, vintage toys, and rare collector items. It is a must-visit for anime and manga fans.

The Akihabara branch is excellent, but serious collectors should also consider **Mandarake in Nakano Broadway**, which is one of Tokyo’s best destinations for vintage and niche collectibles.

**What to look for:**  
- Rare manga editions  
- Anime figures and model kits  
- Vintage character goods  
- Doujinshi and fan-made works  
- Retro video game merchandise  
- Idol and tokusatsu collectibles

**Tip:** Some items are secondhand but in excellent condition. Check item labels carefully, and ask staff before opening sealed products.

---

## 5. Marunouchi & Yurakucho: Architecture, Events & Elegant Shopping

### Tokyo International Forum
**Best for:** Architecture, events, flea markets, nearby shopping  
**Area:** Yurakucho/Marunouchi

Tokyo International Forum is not a conventional shopping mall, but it is worth including in a shopping itinerary because of its dramatic glass architecture, central location, and frequent events. It sits between Yurakucho and Tokyo Station, close to Ginza and Marunouchi shopping areas.

The building often hosts concerts, exhibitions, conventions, craft fairs, and seasonal markets. On some days, you may find antique markets or special event stalls nearby. Even if there is no event, the building is a striking place to walk through and photograph.

**Nearby shopping options:**  
- Ginza department stores and boutiques  
- Marunouchi Brick Square  
- Tokyo Station underground shopping streets  
- Yurakucho electronics and dining areas  
- Mitsukoshi Ginza, within walking distance or a short train ride

**Tip:** Check the event schedule before visiting, as the best shopping opportunities here are usually tied to temporary events.

---

# Suggested One-Day Shopping Itineraries

## Itinerary A: Ginza & Marunouchi Luxury Day
**Best for:** Department stores, luxury brands, food halls, architecture

1. Start at **Mitsukoshi Ginza** for department store shopping and the depachika food hall.  
2. Walk around Ginza’s luxury boutiques and flagship stores.  
3. Visit **Ginza Sony Park / Sony Building area** for design or tech-related events.  
4. Continue to Yurakucho and explore the **Tokyo International Forum**.  
5. End near Tokyo Station or Marunouchi for dinner and refined shopping.

---

## Itinerary B: Harajuku Cute & Fashion Day
**Best for:** Youth fashion, character goods, cafes, street style

1. Arrive at Harajuku Station.  
2. Walk down **Takeshita-Dori** for accessories, snacks, and youth fashion.  
3. Visit **Kiddy Land** near Omotesando for toys and character goods.  
4. Explore **Omotesando** for designer stores, cafes, and stylish architecture.  
5. Continue to Cat Street or Shibuya if you still have energy.

---

## Itinerary C: Akihabara Anime & Electronics Day
**Best for:** Electronics, gaming, manga, anime, collectibles

1. Start at **Yodobashi Camera Akiba** for electronics, cameras, games, and gadgets.  
2. Explore Akihabara’s smaller anime, gaming, and figure shops.  
3. Visit **Mandarake** for manga, collectibles, and rare items.  
4. Try capsule toy machines and arcades in the area.  
5. End with dinner at a themed cafe, ramen shop, or casual izakaya.

---

# Shopping Tips for Tourists in Tokyo

## Tax-Free Shopping
Many larger stores offer tax-free shopping for tourists. You usually need:  
- Your physical passport  
- Purchases above a minimum amount  
- To follow rules about consumables, which may be sealed for export

Tax-free counters can get busy, especially in department stores.

---

## Payment
Credit cards are widely accepted in department stores and major shops, but smaller boutiques, markets, and older stores may prefer cash. IC cards such as Suica or Pasmo are useful for transport and some purchases.

---

## Packing and Luggage
Tokyo shops are excellent for small, high-quality items, but electronics, figures, and toys can take up space quickly. Consider bringing a foldable extra bag or buying luggage at Hands or Yodobashi Camera.

---

## Best Times to Shop
- **Weekday mornings:** Least crowded  
- **Weekends:** Lively but busy, especially Harajuku and Akihabara  
- **Evenings:** Good atmosphere in Ginza, Shibuya, and Shinjuku  
- **New Year season:** Major sales, but also heavy crowds and some closures

---

## Etiquette
- Avoid opening sealed products unless permitted.  
- Ask before taking photos inside stores.  
- Queue politely at registers and tax-free counters.  
- In busy areas like Takeshita-Dori, keep moving and avoid blocking the street for photos.

---

# Quick Area Summary

| Area | Best For | Key Stops |
|---|---|---|
| Ginza | Luxury, cosmetics, food halls, design | Mitsukoshi, Sony Building/Ginza Sony Park |
| Harajuku | Youth fashion, kawaii culture, snacks | Takeshita-Dori, Kiddy Land |
| Omotesando | Designer fashion, cafes, architecture | Omotesando, Omotesando Hills |
| Shibuya/Shinjuku | Lifestyle goods, stationery, travel items | Tokyu Hands/Hands |
| Akihabara | Electronics, anime, games | Yodobashi Camera, Mandarake |
| Yurakucho/Marunouchi | Events, architecture, nearby shopping | Tokyo International Forum |

Tokyo rewards both planned shopping and spontaneous wandering. For a balanced trip, combine one luxury or department store area, one youth-fashion neighborhood, and one specialty district such as Akihabara. This gives you the full range of Tokyo shopping, from elegant Mitsukoshi food halls to Takeshita-Dori street fashion, Kiddy Land character goods, Mandarake collectibles, and Yodobashi Camera electronics.

# Where to shop in Tokyo: Glittering malls, manga meccas and basement food wonderlands

**Tokyo, Japan** — Shopping in Tokyo is less a pastime than a full-sensory expedition. One minute you’re sampling jewel-like sweets in a department-store basement; the next, you’re standing under neon signs in an electronics canyon, flipping through vintage manga or hunting for limited-edition sneakers.

From high-fashion boulevards to weekend flea markets, here are some of the city’s best places to shop — and the neighborhoods that make them worth lingering in.

---

## Ginza: Luxury flagships and legendary depachika

**Best for:** High fashion, cosmetics, gifts, department stores, immaculate food halls  
**Vibe:** Polished, upscale, architectural, elegant

Ginza is Tokyo’s grand shopping stage — a district of gleaming flagships, hushed boutiques and department stores where elevators glide like silk. It’s where global luxury brands sit beside old-school Japanese retailers and some of the city’s finest **depachika** — the famed basement food halls found beneath major department stores.

### Ginza Mitsukoshi  
**Address:** 4-6-16 Ginza, Chuo City, Tokyo 104-8212  
A classic stop for beautifully packaged Japanese sweets, seasonal fruit, bento boxes and edible souvenirs. Head downstairs to the depachika for lacquered displays of wagashi, sushi, grilled meats and delicate cakes.

### Matsuya Ginza  
**Address:** 3-6-1 Ginza, Chuo City, Tokyo 104-8130  
Known for fashion, design goods and cosmetics, Matsuya also has an excellent basement food floor. It’s a strong choice for travelers looking to bring home stylish Japanese kitchenware, stationery or confectionery.

### Ginza Six  
**Address:** 6-10-1 Ginza, Chuo City, Tokyo 104-0061  
A sleek luxury complex with fashion, design boutiques, art installations and a rooftop garden. Even if you’re just browsing, it’s worth visiting for the architecture and curated atmosphere.

---

## Shibuya: Youth fashion, music and pop culture energy

**Best for:** Streetwear, trend shopping, beauty, music, teen fashion  
**Vibe:** Fast-moving, bright, youthful, always changing

Shibuya is Tokyo in motion: giant screens, diagonal crossings, pop-up shops and crowds that seem to pulse with the city’s latest trends. This is the place to browse Japanese and international streetwear, cosmetics, character goods and fashion aimed at younger shoppers.

### Shibuya 109  
**Address:** 2-29-1 Dogenzaka, Shibuya City, Tokyo 150-0043  
A landmark of Japanese youth fashion, Shibuya 109 is packed with compact boutiques selling trend-driven clothing, accessories and beauty items.

### Shibuya Parco  
**Address:** 15-1 Udagawacho, Shibuya City, Tokyo 150-0042  
A must for pop culture fans. Inside you’ll find fashion, design shops, restaurants and a “Tokyo culture” mix that includes anime, gaming and character stores.

### Tower Records Shibuya  
**Address:** 1-22-14 Jinnan, Shibuya City, Tokyo 150-0041  
Still a pilgrimage site for music lovers, with multiple floors of CDs, vinyl, books and merchandise. It’s a reminder that physical media never really went out of style in Tokyo.

---

## Harajuku and Omotesando: Kawaii, street style and designer gloss

**Best for:** Youth culture, fashion, accessories, sneakers, design shopping  
**Vibe:** Playful in Harajuku, polished in Omotesando

A short walk can take you from Harajuku’s candy-colored chaos to Omotesando’s tree-lined elegance. Together, they form one of Tokyo’s most satisfying shopping districts: cute character goods, vintage finds, streetwear, sneakers, beauty boutiques and architectural designer stores.

### Takeshita Street  
**Address:** Around 1 Jingumae, Shibuya City, Tokyo 150-0001  
A narrow pedestrian street famous for kawaii fashion, crepes, accessories and teen trends. Go early if you want breathing room.

### Laforet Harajuku  
**Address:** 1-11-6 Jingumae, Shibuya City, Tokyo 150-0001  
A long-running hub for experimental youth fashion, gothic looks, accessories and indie labels. It’s one of the best places to see Tokyo fashion at its most expressive.

### Omotesando Hills  
**Address:** 4-12-10 Jingumae, Shibuya City, Tokyo 150-0001  
Designed by architect Tadao Ando, this upscale shopping complex offers Japanese and international fashion, lifestyle goods and cafes in a sleek setting.

### Kiddy Land Harajuku  
**Address:** 6-1-9 Jingumae, Shibuya City, Tokyo 150-0001  
One of Tokyo’s great toy stores, stacked with character goods, plush toys, collectibles and gifts. Expect Sanrio, Studio Ghibli, Snoopy, Pokémon-related items and seasonal surprises.

---

## Akihabara: Electronics, anime, manga and otaku treasure hunts

**Best for:** Electronics, gaming, anime, manga, figures, retro tech  
**Vibe:** Neon, nerdy, dense, wonderfully overwhelming

Akihabara is Tokyo’s electric town — a district where electronics shops, manga stores, arcades and collectible figure shops crowd the streets. Whether you’re hunting camera gear, retro games or obscure anime merchandise, Akihabara rewards patience.

### Yodobashi Camera Multimedia Akiba  
**Address:** 1-1 Kanda Hanaokacho, Chiyoda City, Tokyo 101-0028  
A huge electronics department store selling cameras, laptops, appliances, headphones, toys, games and travel gadgets. It’s one of the easiest places for visitors to shop for electronics in Tokyo.

### Mandarake Complex Akihabara  
**Address:** 3-11-12 Sotokanda, Chiyoda City, Tokyo 101-0021  
A multi-floor paradise for manga, anime, doujinshi, toys, figures and collectibles. Serious collectors can lose hours here.

### Radio Kaikan  
**Address:** 1-15-16 Sotokanda, Chiyoda City, Tokyo 101-0021  
A classic Akihabara building filled with shops selling model kits, trading cards, figures, dolls, anime goods and hobby supplies.

---

## Nakano: Manga, collectibles and subculture without the chaos

**Best for:** Manga, vintage toys, anime goods, watches, collectibles  
**Vibe:** Retro, local, maze-like, treasure-filled

If Akihabara is the bright billboard version of otaku culture, Nakano is its slightly scruffier, deeply lovable cousin. The shopping arcades near Nakano Station lead to **Nakano Broadway**, a legendary complex packed with manga, vintage toys, animation cels, model cars, idol goods and collectible watches.

### Nakano Broadway  
**Address:** 5-52-15 Nakano, Nakano City, Tokyo 164-0001  
Home to multiple Mandarake branches and countless specialty stores, Nakano Broadway is one of Tokyo’s best places for secondhand manga, rare toys and vintage pop-culture finds.

### Nakano Sun Mall Shopping Street  
**Address:** 5 Nakano, Nakano City, Tokyo 164-0001  
A covered arcade leading from Nakano Station to Nakano Broadway. It’s lined with casual shops, snack stands, pharmacies and everyday local stores.

---

## Shinjuku: Department stores, depachika and mega-shopping

**Best for:** One-stop shopping, food halls, fashion, beauty, stationery  
**Vibe:** Huge, vertical, energetic, convenient

Shinjuku is a city within the city, with department stores clustered around one of the world’s busiest train stations. It’s ideal if you want everything — luxury goods, mid-range fashion, cosmetics, books, electronics and superb depachika — without traveling far.

### Isetan Shinjuku  
**Address:** 3-14-1 Shinjuku, Shinjuku City, Tokyo 160-0022  
A fashion institution with one of Tokyo’s most celebrated depachika. The basement food hall is a polished theater of patisserie, sushi, tea, premium fruit, bento and gourmet gifts.

### Takashimaya Times Square  
**Address:** 5-24-2 Sendagaya, Shibuya City, Tokyo 151-8580  
Despite the Shibuya City address, this complex sits by Shinjuku Station’s south side. It includes fashion, lifestyle goods, restaurants and a branch of Tokyu Hands.

### NEWoMan Shinjuku  
**Address:** 5-24-55 Sendagaya, Shibuya City, Tokyo 151-0051  
A stylish shopping complex focused on fashion, cosmetics, cafes and quality food gifts, especially convenient for travelers passing through Shinjuku Station.

---

## Ikebukuro: Anime, toys and family-friendly shopping

**Best for:** Anime goods, character shops, toys, department stores  
**Vibe:** Busy, accessible, youthful, slightly more relaxed than Shibuya

Ikebukuro is a major shopping hub with a strong anime and manga scene, particularly around the east side of the station. It’s also home to big department stores, family attractions and character shops.

### Sunshine City  
**Address:** 3-1 Higashiikebukuro, Toshima City, Tokyo 170-8630  
A sprawling complex with shops, restaurants, an aquarium, observation deck and character stores. It’s a good family-friendly stop with plenty to browse.

### Animate Ikebukuro Main Store  
**Address:** 1-20-7 Higashiikebukuro, Toshima City, Tokyo 170-0013  
One of Japan’s flagship anime and manga stores, with floors of comics, character goods, CDs, Blu-rays and event spaces.

### Pokémon Center Mega Tokyo  
**Address:** Sunshine City Alpa 2F, 3-1-2 Higashiikebukuro, Toshima City, Tokyo 170-6002  
A colorful stop for Pokémon plush toys, stationery, games, apparel and exclusive merchandise.

---

## Shimokitazawa: Vintage fashion and indie boutiques

**Best for:** Vintage clothing, secondhand shopping, vinyl, cafes  
**Vibe:** Bohemian, relaxed, creative, local

Shimokitazawa is Tokyo’s indie shopping village: narrow lanes, tiny vintage shops, record stores, coffee spots and small theaters. It’s especially strong for used clothing, from American denim and military jackets to retro dresses and quirky accessories.

### New York Joe Exchange  
**Address:** 5-32-5 Daizawa, Setagaya City, Tokyo 155-0032  
A popular secondhand shop in a converted bathhouse, known for affordable vintage and frequent stock turnover.

### Flamingo Shimokitazawa  
**Address:** 2-25-12 Kitazawa, Setagaya City, Tokyo 155-0031  
A vintage store specializing in colorful American clothing, retro pieces and accessories.

### BONUS TRACK Shimokitazawa  
**Address:** 2-36-15 Daita, Setagaya City, Tokyo 155-0033  
A newer shopping and dining lane with small shops, books, food and relaxed outdoor seating.

---

## Daikanyama and Ebisu: Design, books and grown-up Tokyo style

**Best for:** Design goods, books, lifestyle shopping, cafes  
**Vibe:** Leafy, stylish, calm, sophisticated

For a slower shopping day, head to Daikanyama and nearby Ebisu. This is Tokyo at its softest: low-rise boutiques, bakeries, design stores and carefully edited shelves.

### Daikanyama T-Site  
**Address:** 17-5 Sarugakucho, Shibuya City, Tokyo 150-0033  
A beautifully designed bookstore and lifestyle complex with magazines, books, stationery, music, travel goods and cafes. It’s one of Tokyo’s most pleasant places to browse.

### Log Road Daikanyama  
**Address:** 13-1 Daikanyamacho, Shibuya City, Tokyo 150-0034  
A leafy open-air shopping lane with boutiques, cafes and a relaxed neighborhood feel.

---

## Toyosu and Odaiba: Family shopping, toys and waterfront malls

**Best for:** Families, toys, casual fashion, entertainment complexes  
**Vibe:** Spacious, modern, breezy, waterfront

Tokyo’s bay area offers a more open, mall-style shopping experience — useful for families or anyone who wants wider walkways and entertainment mixed with retail.

### Urban Dock LaLaport Toyosu  
**Address:** 2-4-9 Toyosu, Koto City, Tokyo 135-8614  
A large waterfront mall with fashion, kids’ stores, restaurants and views over Tokyo Bay.

### DiverCity Tokyo Plaza  
**Address:** 1-1-10 Aomi, Koto City, Tokyo 135-0064  
Known for the giant Unicorn Gundam statue outside, this mall offers fashion, character goods, restaurants and entertainment.

### Small Worlds Miniature Museum  
**Address:** 1-3-33 Ariake, Koto City, Tokyo 135-0063  
Not strictly a shopping destination, but its gift shop appeals to toy, model and miniature fans — a good side trip for families and collectors.

---

## Tokyo flea markets: The thrill of the unexpected

**Best for:** Vintage kimono, ceramics, antiques, records, old toys, curios  
**Vibe:** Seasonal, local, unpredictable, bargain-friendly

Tokyo’s flea markets are where the city’s polish gives way to rummaging joy. Schedules change, especially during bad weather, so check official listings before going.

### Oedo Antique Market  
**Address:** Tokyo International Forum, 3-5-1 Marunouchi, Chiyoda City, Tokyo 100-0005  
Usually held on selected Sundays, this is one of Tokyo’s best-known antique markets. Expect ceramics, textiles, vintage kimono, prints, tableware and small collectibles.

### Tokyo City Flea Market  
**Address:** Oi Racecourse, 2-1-2 Katsushima, Shinagawa City, Tokyo 140-0012  
One of the city’s larger flea markets, often held on weekends. Stalls may sell clothing, housewares, toys, records, tools and secondhand odds and ends.

### Yoyogi Park events and markets  
**Address:** 2-1 Yoyogikamizonocho, Shibuya City, Tokyo 151-0052  
Yoyogi Park hosts periodic flea markets, food festivals and cultural events. Pair a market visit with Harajuku or Omotesando shopping nearby.

---

## Don’t miss: Tokyo’s depachika food halls

A Tokyo shopping trip isn’t complete without visiting a **depachika**. These basement food halls are part gourmet market, part culinary theater. Counters sparkle with sushi, tempura, yakitori, salads, fruit tarts, French pastries, Japanese sweets and perfectly packed bento.

Top depachika to try:

- **Isetan Shinjuku** — 3-14-1 Shinjuku, Shinjuku City  
- **Ginza Mitsukoshi** — 4-6-16 Ginza, Chuo City  
- **Matsuya Ginza** — 3-6-1 Ginza, Chuo City  
- **Daimaru Tokyo** — 1-9-1 Marunouchi, Chiyoda City  
- **Nihombashi Takashimaya S.C.** — 2-4-1 Nihombashi, Chuo City  

Go around 5 p.m. for dinner inspiration — or later in the evening, when some prepared foods may be discounted.

---

## Quick guide: Where to shop for what

- **Luxury fashion:** Ginza, Omotesando, Shinjuku  
- **Street fashion:** Harajuku, Shibuya, Shimokitazawa  
- **Manga and anime:** Akihabara, Nakano, Ikebukuro  
- **Electronics:** Akihabara, Shinjuku  
- **Toys and character goods:** Harajuku, Ikebukuro, Odaiba  
- **Vintage clothing:** Shimokitazawa, Koenji, Harajuku backstreets  
- **Food gifts:** Depachika in Ginza, Shinjuku, Tokyo Station  
- **Flea markets and antiques:** Marunouchi, Shinagawa, Yoyogi  

---

## Shopping tips for Tokyo

Bring your passport for tax-free shopping at participating stores, usually when spending above the minimum required amount. Many major retailers accept credit cards, but smaller vintage shops and flea markets may prefer cash. Also, don’t expect much bargaining in regular stores — but at flea markets, polite negotiation may be possible.

And leave room in your suitcase. In Tokyo, the best souvenir is often the thing you didn’t know existed until you saw it: a tiny capsule toy, a perfect melon shortcake, a vintage manga issue, a kitchen knife, a silk scarf or a plastic Gundam kit you suddenly cannot live without.
